summary: Specifies conventions for using the HSS/LMS hash-based signature algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax, including algorithm identifier and public key syntax. HSS/LMS, described in RFC 8554, is a form of hash-based digital signature. It was replaced by RFC 9708.

eli5.summary: This shows how to use a kind of signature built only from hashing in signed messages. It was later replaced by RFC 9708.

subtitle: Hash-based digital signatures in cryptographic messages using HSS/LMS.

tldr.problem: Current digital signature algorithms (RSA, ECDSA) are vulnerable to future quantum computers, and software needs a post-quantum-safe way to sign messages and verify authenticity.
tldr.mechanism: HSS/LMS is a hash-based signature system built from Merkle trees that uses only collision-resistant hash functions (SHA-256), making it secure even against quantum computers. The RFC specifies how to use it within CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) for signed messages.
tldr.outcome: The standard enables deployment of hash-based signatures for critical applications like software updates, but signatures are large and keys can only sign a limited number of messages. It was refined in RFC 9708.

today: RFC 8708 remains an Internet Standard. HSS/LMS signatures are standardized in CMS for use in post-quantum-secure applications like software update signing. The specification was refined by RFC 9708, which provides clarifications and adjustments.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
Recent advances in quantum computing pose a threat to widely deployed digital signature algorithms. RSA, DSA, ECDSA, and EdDSA are all vulnerable to large-scale quantum computers because they depend on the difficulty of discrete logarithms or integer factoring.

The Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) combined with the Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) algorithm is post-quantum secure because it depends only on collision-resistant hash functions, not on mathematical hard problems that quantum computers can solve. HSS/LMS does not depend on the discrete logarithm problem or factoring.

This document specifies how to use HSS/LMS with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), enabling organizations to sign critical software updates and other data with signatures that will remain secure against quantum threats. The algorithm is described in detail in RFC 8554.
sections.eli5: Bad math problems (like factoring big numbers) that quantum computers will break. Good solution: signatures based on hashing, which quantum computers cannot break easily.

sections.title: HSS/LMS Algorithm Structure
sections.content:
HSS/LMS uses a hierarchy of hash-based signature trees to sign many messages efficiently.

At the bottom: The Leighton-Micali One-Time Signature (LM-OTS) algorithm signs one message using a tree of hashed values. Each private key can sign exactly one message. LM-OTS supports four variants with different hash widths (w=1, 2, 4, or 8).

One level up: The Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) system stacks many LM-OTS keys together in a tree. An LMS tree of height h contains 2^h leaves, each an LM-OTS key. The RFC supports five tree heights: h=5 (32 signatures), h=10 (1024), h=15 (32K), h=20 (1M), and h=25 (33M signatures).

At the top: The Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) extends LMS by allowing a hierarchy of trees. The private key of a parent LMS tree signs the public key of a child LMS tree, enabling very large numbers of signatures. For example, a 2-level HSS with h=20 at both levels can sign 1 trillion messages.

All three algorithms exclusively use SHA-256 hashing, producing small public keys but relatively large signatures and consuming moderate computational resources.
sections.eli5: One small hash-based key can sign only one message. Stack many of those keys in a tree to sign thousands. Then stack multiple trees to sign trillions of messages.

sections.title: Use in Cryptographic Message Syntax
sections.content:
CMS is a standard format for cryptographically signed and enveloped messages, used in S/MIME email and many other applications.

When using HSS/LMS with CMS, the algorithm identifier is id-alg-hss-lms-hashsig (OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.3.17), with no parameters.

The public key is encoded as an OCTET STRING containing the number of hierarchy levels (L), followed by the LMS public key data. The public key for the topmost LMS tree serves as the HSS system's public key.

For signed data, the digest algorithm field MUST specify SHA-256 (the only hash function currently supported). The signature field contains the complete HSS signature value, including any hierarchy data and the LMS signature over the message.

When signed attributes are absent, the HSS/LMS signature is computed directly over the content. When signed attributes are present, a digest is computed over the content, then HSS/LMS signs the DER-encoded set of signed attributes (including content-type and message-digest).
sections.eli5: CMS is a format for signed messages. To use HSS/LMS, you put the hierarchy level and public key in the right place, use SHA-256 hashing, and put the signature in the signature field.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST protect HSS/LMS private keys from exposure; compromise allows signature forgery. Additionally, implementations must track which leaf nodes in the tree have been used, since reusing an LM-OTS key breaks security. Loss of integrity of this tracking data (for example, through virtual machine snapshotting without state synchronization) can cause catastrophic key reuse.

Each LMS private key pair must be generated independently. An LM-OTS private key can only be used once for signing; using it more than once exposes the private key.

The RFC emphasizes that random number generation is critical. Poor pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs) for key generation can result in weak keys, and implementation MUST follow RFC 4086 guidance on randomness.

A critical limitation: HSS/LMS signatures are quite large (each signature can be several kilobytes depending on tree height). The algorithm also supports only a finite, predetermined number of signatures based on the tree parameters. Once the tree is exhausted, new keys must be generated. This makes HSS/LMS suitable for scenarios like software update signing (where volume is manageable) but not for high-frequency signing operations.
sections.eli5: Keep the private key secret and tracked carefully. Each key can only sign once. Signatures are big files. The whole system can only sign a fixed number of messages total.
